title: MASLD: Find Fibrosis Risk, Treat Cardiometabolic Disease
bottomLine: The canonical Full-lesson slug uses the older NAFLD term, but current learner-facing care should use metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The NP priority is not merely detecting steatosis; it is identifying advanced-fibrosis risk, treating cardiometabolic drivers and excluding alternate liver disease when the pattern does not fit.
recognize: MASLD commonly accompanies obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and other cardiometabolic risk, and aminotransferases may be normal despite clinically important fibrosis.
Steatosis on imaging is not enough to determine fibrosis stage or future liver risk.
differentiate: Alcohol exposure, viral hepatitis, medications, autoimmune/metabolic liver disease and other steatotic-liver causes can coexist or alter the diagnosis.
Mild AST/ALT elevation does not measure fibrosis severity; advanced disease can have near-normal enzymes.
assessment: Assess cardiometabolic risk, alcohol quantity/pattern, medication/supplement exposure, diabetes, sleep apnea, family liver history and clinical signs of advanced liver disease.
Use non-stigmatizing language and avoid implying that body weight alone defines disease severity.
workup: Use routine liver chemistry plus a validated first-line fibrosis risk strategy such as FIB-4 in the population where it is appropriate; CASL emphasized FIB-4 as a cornerstone of first-line MASLD fibrosis risk stratification in 2026.
Escalate indeterminate/high-risk results to transient elastography or another validated noninvasive fibrosis assessment and hepatology referral rather than serially repeating liver enzymes alone.
management: Treat diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea and cardiovascular risk aggressively; lifestyle/weight interventions should be individualized and evidence based.
Use obesity/diabetes pharmacotherapy or metabolic-bariatric pathways when indicated for the whole patient, not as an isolated liver-number intervention.
Advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis changes surveillance, medication and referral needs.
medicationSafety: Do not withhold statins solely because stable MASLD is present when cardiovascular indication is strong; evaluate true drug-induced liver injury separately.
Avoid unproven supplements marketed as liver detoxification.
counselling: Explain that cardiovascular disease is a major competing risk and that fibrosis—not the amount of fat seen on ultrasound—best predicts liver outcomes.
followUp: Reassess cardiometabolic control and fibrosis risk at evidence-appropriate intervals; patients with advanced fibrosis require hepatology and cirrhosis-specific surveillance.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because AST/ALT are normal despite diabetes, steatosis and a high fibrosis-risk profile.
oneLinePearl: In MASLD, find the fibrosis risk and treat the metabolic risk—not just the fatty liver image.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver 2026 MASLD/FIB-4 advocacy and guidance context

title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease: Assess Severity Without Stigma
bottomLine: The legacy Full slug uses the older 'alcoholic' terminology; learner-facing content should use alcohol-associated liver disease. Establish alcohol exposure and liver-disease severity without moral judgment, distinguish steatosis/hepatitis/cirrhosis and withdrawal risk, and integrate evidence-based alcohol-use-disorder treatment with hepatology care.
recognize: Alcohol-associated steatosis may be silent; progressive disease can cause jaundice, coagulopathy, ascites, encephalopathy, muscle wasting and portal-hypertension complications.
A patient with heavy alcohol exposure can also have viral, metabolic or medication-related liver disease; alcohol history does not close the differential.
differentiate: Alcohol-associated hepatitis is an acute inflammatory clinical syndrome, not simply any AST elevation after drinking.
Withdrawal risk and liver decompensation are separate acute problems and may coexist.
assessment: Use a nonjudgmental alcohol history including quantity, pattern, last use, prior withdrawal/seizure, other substances, nutrition, psychiatric risk and readiness for treatment.
Assess jaundice, bleeding, ascites, infection, encephalopathy and signs of withdrawal or severe malnutrition.
workup: Use CBC, liver chemistry, bilirubin, INR, renal function/electrolytes and cause-directed testing; evaluate viral/other liver disease when appropriate.
Use fibrosis/portal-hypertension assessment and imaging according to disease stage; severity scores can support specialty decisions but do not replace bedside assessment.
management: Alcohol cessation is central, but safe management may require medically supervised withdrawal and addiction treatment rather than a simple instruction to stop immediately at home.
Treat malnutrition and liver complications; severe alcohol-associated hepatitis or decompensation requires hospital/hepatology assessment.
Offer evidence-based AUD pharmacotherapy and psychosocial/addiction supports matched to liver/renal status and patient goals.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepine choice/dosing for withdrawal must account for liver dysfunction and respiratory/sedation risk.
AUD medications have liver/renal/interaction considerations; verify the selected agent against current Canadian guidance rather than assuming all are interchangeable.
counselling: Use person-first language, discuss relapse as a treatable chronic-disease event and connect abstinence/reduction goals with concrete addiction supports.
followUp: Track alcohol-use treatment, nutrition, liver recovery and cirrhosis complications; close referral loops with addiction medicine/hepatology.
examTrap: Telling a dependent patient with prior withdrawal seizures to 'just stop drinking tonight' without a withdrawal-safety plan.
oneLinePearl: Treat the liver disease and the alcohol-use disorder together—and do both without stigma.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver alcohol-associated liver disease practice resources
Canadian Guideline for Clinical Management of High-Risk Drinking and Alcohol Use Disorder

title: Cirrhosis: Compensated or Decompensated Changes Everything
bottomLine: Cirrhosis becomes decompensated when complications such as ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice emerge. Manage the precipitant and complication, avoid kidney- and brain-worsening medications, provide HCC/variceal surveillance and refer appropriate patients for transplant assessment before repeated crises become the norm.
recognize: Portal hypertension can produce thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, varices and ascites; decompensation includes ascites, HE, variceal hemorrhage and jaundice.
Infection and AKI may present subtly and can precipitate encephalopathy or rapid deterioration.
differentiate: Peripheral edema/ascites in cirrhosis is not managed like uncomplicated heart-failure edema; spontaneous bacterial peritonitis must be considered in new/worsening ascites with illness.
A high INR in cirrhosis does not straightforwardly mean the patient is 'auto-anticoagulated' or protected from thrombosis.
assessment: Assess mental status, bleeding, infection, abdominal pain, ascites/edema, renal function, sodium, nutrition, alcohol/medications and transplant-relevant comorbidity.
Review NSAIDs, sedatives, diuretics, lactulose use and adherence.
workup: Use liver/renal/electrolyte/CBC testing and ultrasound/HCC surveillance according to current cirrhosis guidance.
Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated in appropriate new/worsening ascites or hospitalized/decompensated presentations to assess for SBP; do not rely on fever alone.
management: Manage ascites with sodium strategy, appropriate diuretics and paracentesis/albumin when indicated; treat SBP promptly and use prophylaxis only for evidence-supported risk groups.
Use endoscopic/nonselective-beta-blocker strategies for variceal prevention according to portal-hypertension risk.
Refer recurrent decompensation or appropriate severity for transplant evaluation.
medicationSafety: Avoid NSAIDs in decompensated cirrhosis/ascites because renal and bleeding risk is high; sedatives can worsen encephalopathy.
Diuresis that causes hypotension, hyponatremia or AKI should prompt reassessment rather than automatic escalation.
counselling: Teach early signs of HE, infection and bleeding, medication avoidance, nutrition and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: Maintain HCC/variceal surveillance and monitor renal function, sodium, nutrition and transplant candidacy after each decompensation.
examTrap: Increasing diuretics for ascites while creatinine is rising and blood pressure is falling.
oneLinePearl: In cirrhosis, every new ascites/HE/bleeding episode is a decompensation signal—and a trigger to reassess prognosis and transplant needs.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver cirrhosis/portal-hypertension educational resources

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Find the Precipitant, Treat the Brain-Gut Syndrome
bottomLine: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a clinical neuropsychiatric syndrome in advanced liver disease after competing causes of altered mental status are considered. Look immediately for precipitants such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration/AKI, electrolyte disturbance and sedating drugs; treat overt HE and prevent recurrence rather than ordering ammonia levels as the main diagnostic test.
recognize: Sleep-wake reversal, inattention, personality/behaviour change, disorientation, asterixis and reduced consciousness can occur.
Overt HE can fluctuate; subtle/covert impairment can affect driving, falls and medication adherence.
differentiate: Delirium from sepsis, intracranial disease, hypoglycemia/electrolytes, withdrawal and medication toxicity must remain in the differential.
An elevated ammonia level does not establish HE severity or prove HE is the cause of confusion; a normal value can prompt diagnostic reconsideration but bedside diagnosis remains central.
assessment: Assess airway/mental status, infection, GI bleeding, stool/constipation, hydration/renal function, electrolytes, sedatives/opioids/benzodiazepines and recent diuretic changes.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver tests, glucose, infection/bleeding studies and imaging only as indicated by competing diagnoses.
Do not order serial ammonia levels to monitor clinical response.
management: Treat the precipitant and use lactulose for overt HE, titrated to clinical response and regular soft stools rather than causing severe diarrhea/dehydration.
Add rifaximin for appropriate recurrent overt HE prevention and coordinate hepatology/transplant evaluation when decompensation is recurrent.
Protect airway and escalate severe HE to hospital/critical care.
medicationSafety: Excess lactulose can cause dehydration/electrolyte disturbance and worsen the precipitating physiology.
Avoid unnecessary benzodiazepines, sedatives and opioids that worsen mental status; review renal/hepatic accumulation.
counselling: Teach patients/caregivers early cognitive/behaviour warning signs, bowel-plan goals and the need to report infection, bleeding or dehydration.
followUp: After recovery, document precipitant, recurrence-prevention plan and transplant/hepatology follow-up.
examTrap: Diagnosing and grading HE from the ammonia level while missing sepsis, GI bleeding or sedative toxicity.
oneLinePearl: HE is clinical: find the precipitant, treat with lactulose appropriately, and do not chase ammonia numbers.
sourceBasis: Canadian hepatology practice resources for hepatic encephalopathy

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Diagnose Correctly, Resuscitate Thoughtfully, Feed Early
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when the clinical picture satisfies the accepted diagnostic criteria—not from lipase alone. Assess severity/organ failure, give goal-directed crystalloid and analgesia, identify gallstone/alcohol/triglyceride/drug and other causes, start oral/enteral feeding as tolerated, and reserve antibiotics/procedures for defined complications rather than routine use.
recognize: Acute persistent epigastric pain often radiating to the back with nausea/vomiting is typical, but older/pregnant/critically ill patients may vary.
Elevated lipase supports diagnosis but does not grade severity and can occur in other abdominal/renal/critical illness.
differentiate: Biliary disease, perforated ulcer, mesenteric ischemia, ACS and other acute abdominal causes can mimic pancreatitis.
Pancreatic necrosis is not automatically infected; fever/inflammation early can be sterile.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, urine output, oxygenation, mental status, volume depletion, SIRS/organ dysfunction, alcohol, gallstone symptoms, medications and triglyceride risk.
workup: Use lipase and targeted labs including liver chemistry, renal/electrolytes, CBC/glucose/triglycerides when indicated; ultrasound evaluates gallstones/biliary dilation.
Routine early CT is not required when diagnosis is clear; use CT/MRI for diagnostic uncertainty or complications/failed improvement according to timing and severity.
management: Provide individualized crystalloid resuscitation with frequent reassessment to avoid under-resuscitation or overload, plus adequate analgesia and antiemetics.
Begin oral/enteral nutrition early as tolerated; do not keep uncomplicated pancreatitis NPO until enzymes normalize.
Urgent ERCP is indicated for pancreatitis with cholangitis or selected persistent obstruction, not for every gallstone pancreatitis case.
medicationSafety: Do not give prophylactic antibiotics for sterile uncomplicated/necrotizing pancreatitis without infection indication.
Opioid analgesia may be appropriate but requires respiratory/sedation monitoring and should not be withheld based on obsolete sphincter-of-Oddi dogma.
counselling: Address the cause—gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides, medication—and explain recurrence prevention.
followUp: Ensure definitive biliary management when indicated and reassess nutrition, diabetes/exocrine function after severe/recurrent disease.
examTrap: Starting antibiotics and ordering immediate CT for every patient solely because lipase is high.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis care is severity, fluids, pain, early feeding and cause control—not enzyme chasing.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Biochemistry/Gastroenterology recommendations

title: Gallbladder Disease: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, Cholangitis, or CBD Stone?
bottomLine: Right-upper-quadrant pain is a syndrome before it is 'gallstones.' Distinguish transient biliary colic from acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis and ascending cholangitis using pain duration, systemic illness, liver chemistry and ultrasound; cholangitis or obstruction with organ dysfunction needs urgent antibiotics and biliary source control.
recognize: Biliary colic is episodic postprandial RUQ/epigastric pain without persistent inflammatory features; cholecystitis causes more sustained pain/tenderness and inflammatory findings.
Jaundice/cholestatic chemistry or duct dilation raises CBD obstruction; fever+jaundice+RUQ pain or organ dysfunction raises cholangitis.
differentiate: Hepatitis, pancreatitis, peptic disease, renal/pulmonary/cardiac causes can mimic RUQ pain.
Gallstones found incidentally do not prove they are causing nonspecific abdominal symptoms.
assessment: Assess pain duration, fever, jaundice, vomiting, hemodynamics, pregnancy, prior attacks, pancreatitis history and medication/anticoagulation context.
workup: Use RUQ ultrasound first-line for gallstones/cholecystitis and pair with CBC, bilirubin, ALP/GGT/AST/ALT and lipase as clinically indicated.
Use MRCP/EUS or ERCP selectively based on probability of CBD stone/obstruction; ERCP is primarily therapeutic when obstruction/cholangitis is established.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetic support and surgical referral for symptomatic stones/acute cholecystitis according to severity.
Cholangitis requires prompt antibiotics plus urgent biliary drainage/source control.
Uncomplicated asymptomatic gallstones generally do not require prophylactic surgery.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice depends on severity, local resistance, allergy and renal/hepatic function; do not continue broad therapy after source control without indication.
Pregnancy changes imaging/procedural planning but does not justify ignoring cholecystitis/cholangitis.
counselling: Explain the difference between incidental stones and symptomatic biliary disease and provide return precautions for fever/jaundice/persistent pain.
followUp: Ensure surgical/biliary follow-up after symptomatic disease and definitive management after gallstone pancreatitis/cholecystitis when indicated.
examTrap: Sending home a jaundiced febrile patient with RUQ pain as 'biliary colic.'
oneLinePearl: Stones are common; obstruction and infection determine urgency.

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Average-Risk Screening Is Not Symptom Workup
bottomLine: Screening applies to asymptomatic average-risk people; bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, altered bowel habit with alarm features or unexplained weight loss requires diagnostic evaluation instead. Canadian recommendations and provincial programs are changing in 2026: national cancer-society guidance now supports stool-based screening from 45 to 74 for average risk, while publicly funded program ages vary by province/territory.
recognize: Average-risk screening is usually stool-test based at regular intervals; colonoscopy is used for abnormal screening tests and higher-risk/surveillance pathways rather than as the default population screening test everywhere.
Family history, hereditary syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease and prior advanced polyps move the patient out of average-risk screening.
differentiate: A FIT is a screening test for an asymptomatic patient, not the appropriate diagnostic response to overt rectal bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia.
Provincial funded-program eligibility and national evidence recommendations are not always identical during implementation changes.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then age, family/personal polyp/cancer history, IBD, hereditary risk, prior screening results and access/follow-up barriers.
workup: For average risk, use the current provincial/territorial organized program and current Canadian evidence; an abnormal stool screen requires timely colonoscopy.
Symptomatic/high-risk patients need a diagnostic or surveillance pathway independent of routine screening intervals.
management: Offer evidence-supported screening with shared decision-making and ensure the patient can complete follow-up after an abnormal result.
Do not repeat FIT after a positive result as a substitute for colonoscopy.
Address access, disability, language and transportation barriers that reduce screening completion.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet management before colonoscopy/polypectomy is procedure- and thrombotic-risk specific; use current endoscopy guidance rather than one universal hold rule.
redFlags: Persistent bowel-habit change with alarm features
counselling: Explain screening versus diagnosis and that a positive stool test is not a cancer diagnosis but must be followed with colonoscopy.
followUp: Track abnormal screening until diagnostic resolution; after colonoscopy, surveillance interval is determined by pathology/quality/family-risk rather than returning automatically to average-risk screening.
examTrap: Ordering or repeating FIT for a symptomatic patient with rectal bleeding instead of switching to a diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms = screening; symptoms or prior high-risk findings = diagnosis/surveillance.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cancer Society colorectal cancer screening guidance reviewed March 2026
Provincial and territorial organized colorectal screening programs
